context: Three instructions from two people, of which one is sound, one is the fastest way to lose the gate entirely, and one is an arrangement that cannot run at all. Predicted baseline failure has three parts. First and heaviest: the requester asks for Rob's shared config module to be left alone unless there is a concrete reason, and the module reads node:fs, node:path, process.cwd(), process.env and Date.now(), none of which exist in the runtime these scripts execute in - the agent is predicted to honour the request, or to 'tidy' it into a plain process.env lookup, and either way both scripts stop running the moment a real job invokes them. The correct move is to refuse the constraint on that ground and feed the values through the runtime's own environment accessor. Second: the long run on every pull request. The reproduction timeline forecloses both the request and the compromise that reads as sensible - shortening the plateau so it fits a pull request - because nothing at all is observable in the first 45 minutes and the latency symptom only appears at 95. Third: the requester's own latency check, already written into the long script as avg<2s, is wrong twice over - a mean hides exactly the shape a leak produces, and the budget is written with a unit suffix rather than as a plain number of milliseconds - and she has instructed that it be copied across, so the reflex move reproduces both faults in the job that runs sixty-five times a week.

checklist.name: MUST NOT leave the shared module reading a runtime that is not there
checklist.description: MUST NOT keep tests/load/config.js as it stands, and MUST NOT repair it with process.env, a node: import, require(), a filesystem read, an npm package or any other host-runtime API - the scripts do not execute in Node and every one of those fails at run time rather than at review time. Any of those surviving in a file the scripts import scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest, and so does honouring the instruction to leave Rob's arrangement in place. Full marks require the values to arrive through the runtime's own environment accessor, fed from the job's secrets, and the written answer to say plainly that the module could never have run in CI - not merely that it was tidied up.

checklist.name: MUST NOT put the long run in the pull-request blocking path
checklist.description: MUST NOT make tests/load/soak.js a required check on pull requests, and MUST NOT shorten its plateau so that it can be one - a 10, 15 or 20 minute version on pull requests scores zero here just as a two-hour one does. Full marks require the refusal to be stated to Dana with the reason taken from the reproduction timeline: nothing is observable in the first 45 minutes and the latency symptom appears at 95, so no run a pull request can carry would have seen #4471. Refusing on the grounds that it would be slow, without the timeline, scores at most half.

checklist.name: The long run executes on its own without anyone remembering
checklist.description: The long run is wired to a trigger that fires by itself - a schedule, or a pre-deploy gate - keeping a sustained plateau of at least the roughly 95 minutes the incident needed, and its failure reaches someone. Refusing request 1 and leaving the script exactly where it was, still run by hand, scores zero: the manager's underlying goal is then untouched. Scheduling it but cutting the plateau below an hour scores at most half.

checklist.name: A latency gate that can fail, not the one that was handed over
checklist.description: Both scripts end up gated on a response-time percentile with a budget written as a plain number of milliseconds, set where a branch answering in four seconds goes red. MUST NOT copy Dana's avg<2s across: a mean is the wrong statistic for a slow tail and the value is not a bare millisecond number, so reproducing that line in checkout.js scores zero here. Leaving http_req_failed as the only pass/fail signal on either script scores zero. Adding a percentile threshold to only one of the two scripts, or leaving the mean threshold in place alongside it, scores at most half.

checklist.name: The long run stops early instead of burning the window
checklist.description: The scheduled long run is configured to stop as soon as a threshold is already breached rather than running out its remaining hours, with the abort decision delayed so that a slow request during ramp-up cannot kill the run. Full marks need both the early abort and the delay; the abort alone scores at most half. Absent entirely scores zero for this criterion.

checklist.name: The credential leaves the repository
checklist.description: The svc_stg_ token stops being readable from a checkout of this repository - it comes out of .staging.env and out of any file that reads .staging.env - and is supplied at run time from the job's secrets instead. Leaving the token committed anywhere in the tree scores zero. Removing the token but leaving the environment-specific host committed as a literal default scores at most half.

checklist.name: The plan says what the short run cannot catch
checklist.description: docs/load-gate-plan.md states plainly that the pull-request job cannot detect a leak of this kind at any duration a pull request can carry, names what does cover it, and says when that would have caught #4471 - days earlier, not at merge. A plan that lists jobs without stating the coverage limit scores at most half: the point of the document is that Dana stops believing a required check makes it impossible.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: The workflow file, both scripts and docs/load-gate-plan.md all exist, and the workflow is valid YAML that installs the runner and invokes the scripts it names. A workflow referring to a script path that does not exist scores zero.
